title: What the reformers asked
hook: grace, scripture, and real abuses; Catholics today admit many of the abuses were real

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Reformation, which began as a list for debate. Your line was a monk wanted reform.

A papal envoy stands before a German assembly with a message from the new pope, Adrian the Sixth. Instead of a defense, the envoy reads out a confession. The pope's instruction admits that for years there had been grave abuses in the Holy See itself, that the sickness had spread from the head to the members, and that the pope means to begin the cure at home. A pope, in the middle of the storm, saying: some of this is our fault. So what did the reformers ask?
screen: `AN ENVOY, A CONFESSION.` → `FROM THE HEAD TO THE MEMBERS.` → `WHAT DID THEY ASK?`

segments.voice: They asked three kinds of things. First, grace. Luther read Paul's letter to the Romans, which in the Douay-Rheims says, "The just man liveth by faith." He came to believe we are made right with God by grace, received through faith, not earned. Catholics also teach that grace comes first and can't be bought; the real disagreements were about how grace works in a person, and those took longer to sort out. Second, scripture. The reformers wanted the Bible in ordinary people's hands and languages, and held it to be the final rule over every church teaching. Catholics hold scripture and tradition together, read within the Church. That disagreement is real, and it's still discussed. Third, the abuses, where the reformers were often simply right. Some bishops drew income from dioceses they rarely saw. Church offices were bought and sold. Some priests had barely been taught. And indulgences had been marketed like a product. Pope Adrian's instruction said as much, and so did Catholic reformers inside the Church, before and after Luther. Then, why it matters. You can disagree with the reformers about grace or scripture and still say plainly: they saw real wounds. The Second Vatican Council said that for the separations, often enough, people on both sides were to blame. Honest reform can start with that kind of admission.
screen: `FIRST: GRACE, NOT EARNED.` · `SECOND: SCRIPTURE IN EVERY HAND.` · `THIRD: THE ABUSES.` · `HONESTY BEFORE REFORM.` · then, large: `THE ABUSES WERE REAL.`

segments.voice: Let your week pass before you, what you said, what you spent, how you treated the people closest to you, and look for one habit in you that's drifted, the way an office drifts into a privilege. Don't fix it yet; just name it in one honest sentence, the way Pope Adrian's letter named the abuses. If you pray, bring that sentence before God.
Luther. The reformer who read Paul on grace, called for scripture in everyone's hands, and pointed to abuses the Church needed to face. Today's word.
Your line: the abuses were real. Hearing the true part of a criticism is where honest reform begins. Day seven hundred eighty-two, done.

howItsDone: Catholic and Protestant theologians continue to discuss grace, scripture and authority in formal dialogues; Catholic leaders have publicly acknowledged that abuses in the Church of that era were real.

fork.setup: you're a new pope. a reform movement is tearing the West apart, and some of its complaints about Rome are true. what do you send?
options: a flat denial of every charge.
an admission that the sickness began at the head, and a promise to cure it at home.
fork.reveal: Adrian VI's instruction admitted grave abuses in the Holy See and said the cure would begin there.

what a scholar hears: Adrian VI's instruction to his legate, admitting the corruption had spread from the head to the members.

chat.says: Were the reformers just troublemakers, or did they have a point?
options: On the abuses they were often right; even Pope Adrian the Sixth admitted grave wrongs.
They had no point; Catholic leaders at the time denied that any abuses existed.
Their one complaint was Latin; once Mass was in German, they were satisfied.
chat.meaning: Offices were bought, bishops absent, indulgences marketed. Pope Adrian's instruction admitted the sickness spread from the head; you can disagree on doctrine and still name real wounds.

papal envoy.meaning: a messenger sent on the pope's behalf

Adrian the Sixth.meaning: the pope whose instruction admitted abuses in the Holy See

Holy See.meaning: the pope's office and seat of authority in Rome

dioceses.meaning: areas of the Church, each led by a bishop

Romans.meaning: Paul's letter to the church in Rome

sources.quoted: The just man liveth by faith.

sources.ref: Instruction of Adrian VI to the legate Chieregati, Diet of Nuremberg

notes: Adrian VI's instruction to Francesco Chieregati, read at the Diet of Nuremberg (1522–23), paraphrased: 'for some years many abominations... in this Holy See', 'the sickness has spread from the head to the members'. Confirm wording and that the envoy read it out.
The three kinds of request (grace, scripture, abuses) follow the index hook; the summary of each side is simplified. Confirm fairness to Lutheran and Reformed positions.
Examples of abuses (pluralism of benefices, simony, poorly taught clergy, marketed indulgences): confirm.
'Catholic reformers inside the Church, before and after Luther': confirm acceptable without names.
'Catholic leaders today say so': general claim per the index hook; Keeper may prefer a specific citation.
The index word is the title head 'What the reformers asked', kept exactly.
